headline: Social media addiction lawsuit against Meta is dropped days before trial
summary: The plaintiff, a 15-year-old, withdrew the case after settling with other platforms, allowing Meta to avoid a settlement in this bellwether trial.
details: Just days before a bellwether trial was set to begin, the plaintiff in a social media addiction lawsuit against Meta dropped their case. This means Meta will not have to pay a settlement in this specific trial, unlike other social media companies involved.

The case, brought by a 15-year-old identified as R.K.C., aimed to test legal arguments that social media platforms create addictive features harmful to teens. R.K.C.'s lawyers stated he withdrew to focus on recovery and therapy after settling with TikTok, Snap, and YouTube for undisclosed amounts.

Meta spokesperson Andy Stone affirmed that "The claims never held up," and the company would continue to defend against "baseless lawsuits." This outcome marks a win for Meta in this particular legal battle.

However, Meta and other tech giants still face numerous other legal challenges regarding social media's alleged harms. Meta and Google's YouTube previously lost a different bellwether case, ordered to pay $6 million, and a New Mexico jury ordered Meta to pay a $375 million penalty in a separate case.

There are seven more bellwether cases scheduled in California state court, alongside a separate set of cases in federal court. Meta is also set to face claims from state attorneys general next month regarding allegedly addictive features.

headline: US outlines its $5 billion Genesis Mission to boost science with AI
summary: The White House and Department of Energy detailed the Genesis Mission, a multi-agency initiative with over $5 billion committed to leverage AI for scientific discoveries.
details: The Genesis Mission, established by executive order last November, aims to utilize AI to accelerate scientific discoveries across various fields. Over $5 billion has been committed to this interdisciplinary research effort.

Led by the Department of Energy, at least 15 federal agencies are involved, including the Departments of Health and Human Services, Transportation, Interior, NASA, and the National Science Foundation.

Participants will address National Science and Technology Challenges, focusing on areas like finding root causes of chronic disease, scaling the energy grid, and early detection of biological threats. Other challenges cover microelectronics, biology, weapons, space, quantum computing, and materials science.

Corporate partners are also contributing; Microsoft has launched SPARK (Scientific Partnership Advancing Research & Knowledge) to coordinate research. Microsoft is also providing cloud computing and AI credits to support the mission.
